text: Every Business Rule has a When field with four real options: before, after, async, and display. This isn't a cosmetic setting. It changes exactly when your script runs relative to the database write, and in some cases, whether the write even happens at all.

A before rule runs inside the same transaction, before the record is actually written. Because the write hasn't happened yet, a before rule can still change fields on the current record, and those changes are automatically included in the save. A before rule can also call set abort action true, which cancels the entire operation. No other timing can do that.

An after rule runs once the database write has already committed successfully. That timing exists for one practical reason: it's the safe place to touch other, related records, because the triggering record is already durably saved. Here, an after rule on incident updates work notes on related change requests, now that the incident itself is safe.

Four timings, four different jobs. Before, for changing or aborting the current save. After, for safely updating related records. Async, which also runs after the write, but queued in the background so slow work like notifications or integrations doesn't make the user wait. And display, which is the odd one out entirely.

A display Business Rule doesn't run on save at all. It runs when the form loads, on the server, before the page renders in the browser. Its real purpose is getting server-computed data to the client without a round trip, and the standard pattern is writing values onto an object called g underscore scratchpad, which client scripts can then read directly.

Choosing the right timing is half the skill of writing a good Business Rule. Next, we'll look at what happens when there's more than one rule on the same table — the order field, and the real sequence the platform follows from before, to the write, to after, to async.
